quote: we must take up what Kant himself says about the concept
claim: To understand what a concept is fundamentally, one must examine Kant's own statements about the concept

quote: Every intuition, he says, is a representatio singularis
claim: According to Kant, every intuition is a singular representation (representatio singularis)

quote: The concept, howev­er, is also a representatio, a 'self-presenting,' but, in this case, a representatio per notas communes
claim: According to Kant, the concept is a representation through common marks (representatio per notas communes)

quote: The concept is distinguished from intuition by the fact that, as a presenting, it presents something that has the character of generality
claim: The concept differs from intuition in that it presents something with the character of generality

quote: It is a 'general representation.'
claim: According to Kant, a concept is a general representation

quote: in every cognition, matter is to be distinguished from form, 'the manner in which we cognize the object.'
claim: According to Kant, in every cognition, matter must be distinguished from form (the manner of cognizing the object)

quote: A savage sees a house and, unlike us, does not know its for-what; he has a different 'concept' of the house than we who know our way around in it
claim: A savage who sees a house but does not know its purpose has a different concept of the house than someone who knows its use

quote: he sees the same being, but the knowledge of the use escapes him; he does not understand what he should do with it
claim: The savage perceives the same object but lacks knowledge of its use and does not understand what to do with it

quote: He forms no concept of house
claim: Without knowledge of use, one does not form a concept of the thing

quote: We know what it is for, and thus we represent something general to ourselves
claim: Knowing what something is for enables us to represent something general to ourselves

quote: We who know the use that one could make of it have the concept of house
claim: Having a concept of something requires knowing the use that can be made of it

quote: The concept goes beyond answering the question of what the object is
claim: The concept exceeds merely answering what the object is

quote: The conceptuality and the sense of the concept depend on how one un­derstands, in general, the question concerning what something is
claim: The nature and sense of the concept depend on how one understands the question of what something is

quote: The concept yields what the object, the res, is in the explic­itness of the definition
claim: The concept yields what the object (res) is through the explicitness of definition

quote: the genuine definition is the so-called 'real definition,' which thus determines what the res in itself is
claim: The genuine definition is the 'real definition' which determines what the res is in itself

quote: Definitio is fulfilled through the specification of differences in genus and species
claim: Definition is accomplished through specifying differences in genus and species

quote: At first glance, this procedure seems odd in this context; one does not immediately understand why in particular the genus and the species should determine the object in its What
claim: It is not immediately obvious why genus and species should determine the object in its What

quote: Kant now says that, to be sure, the real definition has the task of determining the What of the matter from the 'first ground' of its 'possibility'
claim: According to Kant, the real definition must determine the What of the matter from the first ground of its possibility

quote: or of determining the matter according to its 'inner possibility.'
claim: Kant holds that real definition determines the matter according to its inner possibility

quote: the determination of the definition, as occurring through genus proximum et differentiam specificam, only counts for the 'nominal definition' that is gen­erated by comparison
claim: According to Kant, definition through genus proximum and differentia specifica applies only to nominal definition, which is generated by comparison

quote: precisely in the case of the definition of the res, this way of determining does not come into play
claim: For Kant, the method of genus and species does not apply to the definition of the res (real definition)

quote: For Kant's position, the two characteristic aspects are (1) that the definitio is discussed in the doctrine of method
claim: A characteristic aspect of Kant's position is that definition is discussed in the doctrine of method

quote: (2) that he determines the basic pro­cedure of the definitio in such a way that it does not come into play for genuine definition
claim: Kant determines the basic procedure of definition such that it does not apply to genuine (real) definition

quote: How does it really come about that the definitio determines the being in its being?
claim: There is a question to be investigated about how definitio determines being in its being

quote: How does it come about that a definitio, which is genuine knowledge of the matter, becomes a matter of logical perfection?
claim: There is a question about how definitio as genuine knowledge became reduced to logical perfection

quote: In this, Kant's position on definitio, lies the fate of Aristotelian research.
claim: Kant's position on definitio embodies the fate (endpoint or destiny) of Aristotelian research

quote: definitio is ορισμός
claim: The Latin term definitio corresponds to the Greek term horismos

quote: ορισμός is a λόγος, a "self-expression" about being-there as being
claim: Horismos is a logos, understood as self-expression about being-there as being

quote: Ορισμός is not a way of apprehending through sharp determination
claim: Horismos should not be understood as apprehending through sharp determination

quote: the specific character of ορισμός ultimately arises from the fact that the being itself is determined in its being as circumscribed by the πέρας
claim: The character of horismos derives from the fact that being is determined by being circumscribed by peras (limit)

quote: Being means being-completed.
claim: Being means being-completed

quote: according to traditional logic, the concept is expressed in the genuine sense through definition
claim: Traditional logic holds that the concept is genuinely expressed through definition

quote: in the definition the concept comes to itself
claim: In definition, the concept comes to itself (achieves full expression)

quote: The concept is, for Kant, distinguished from intuition insofar as intuition simply sees an individual in its being-there
claim: For Kant, intuition simply sees an individual in its being-there

quote: while the concept sees the same object but, so to speak, understands it
claim: For Kant, the concept sees the same object as intuition but understands it

quote: In the representatio of the concept, I know what one understands by it, and another also knows
claim: The concept's representatio involves knowledge that can be shared with others

quote: the concept makes the represented intelligible for others too, and thus it is a general representation
claim: The concept is a general representation because it makes the represented intelligible to others

quote: The concept of a represented res makes the represented matter intelligible to others also; it represents the matter with a certain bindingness
claim: The concept represents matter with bindingness (normative force) making it intelligible to others

quote: The definition should yield a matter in such a way that it is represented and understood in the ground of its possibility
claim: Definition should present a matter as understood in the ground of its possibility

quote: that I know whence it comes, what it is, why it is that
claim: Genuine definition provides knowledge of origin, essence, and reason

quote: The genuine definition is that of the matter, the real definition
claim: Genuine definition is real definition (definition of the matter itself)

quote: In the Middle Ages, genuine definition is the real and essential definition
claim: Medieval philosophy identified genuine definition as real and essential definition

quote: It is genuine and is accomplished insofar as the basic procedure of definition is satisfied, insofar as one specifies the penultimate type or genus of an object, as well as its specific difference
claim: Genuine definition is accomplished by specifying the genus and specific difference of an object

quote: a circle is a closed, curved line (genus), on which every point is equidistant from the center (specific difference)
claim: Example of definition: circle = closed curved line (genus) with all points equidistant from center (differentia)

quote: homo animal (genus) rationale (specific difference)
claim: Example of definition: human = animal (genus) rational (differentia)

quote: We go back to Aristotle in order to show that what, in traditional logic, is treated as definitio has a fully determinate origin
claim: The purpose of returning to Aristotle is to show that definitio in traditional logic has a specific origin

quote: definition is a symptom of decline
claim: Definition (as traditionally conceived) is a symptom of decline

quote: a mere thought technique that was once the basic possibility of human speech
claim: Definition has become a mere thought technique but was originally a basic possibility of human speech

quote: In the definition, the concept becomes explicit. Still, what the concept itself is in its conceptuality is not yet visible
claim: Definition makes the concept explicit, but the conceptuality of the concept itself remains hidden

quote: We do not want to merely become acquainted with Aristotelian basic concepts
claim: The aim is not mere acquaintance with Aristotelian basic concepts

quote: What authorized the return to definition was the fact that, according to traditional logic, the concept is expressed in the genuine sense through definition
claim: The return to definition is justified by traditional logic's view that concepts are genuinely expressed through definition

quote: this concept interests us in its conceptuality
claim: The concept of movement is of interest not for comparative historical purposes but specifically in terms of its conceptuality

quote: We must, therefore, ask what is meant by the concept of movement, in the sense of that which is concretely experienced in the concept as it is meant
claim: The inquiry into the concept of movement must focus on what is concretely experienced in how the concept is meant

quote: What did Aristotle have in mind when he thought of movement? Which mov­ing phenomena did he have in view?
claim: To understand Aristotle's concept of movement, we must identify which moving phenomena Aristotle had in view

quote: We do not ask these questions with the aim of gaining knowledge of a conceptual content, but rather we ask how the matter meant is experienced
claim: The proper inquiry into concepts asks how the matter is experienced rather than seeking mere conceptual content

quote: That which is originally seen is primarily addressed. How does Aristotle take the phenomenon of movement?
claim: The second methodological concern is how that which is originally seen is primarily addressed

quote: Does he clarify movement by way of con­cepts or theories that are already available
claim: One possibility is that Aristotle clarifies movement through pre-existing concepts or theories

quote: perhaps Platonistically, lead him to say that movement is a transition from a nonbeing to a being
claim: A Platonistic approach would characterize movement as a transition from nonbeing to being

quote: Or is it that those determinations that arise for him lie in the phenomenon itself?
claim: An alternative is that Aristotle's determinations of movement arise from the phenomenon itself

quote: In what way is a phenomenon like movement addressed so as to accord with the guiding claim of the matter seen?
claim: How a phenomenon is addressed should accord with the guiding claim of the matter seen

quote: How is the phenomenon thus seen unfolded more precisely; into what sort of conceptuality is it, as it were, spoken?
claim: The third methodological concern is how the seen phenomenon is unfolded into conceptuality

quote: What claim of intelligibility is demanded of that which is thus seen?
claim: The unfolding of a phenomenon into conceptuality involves a specific claim of intelligibility

quote: Is the explication proposed to the phenomenon, or is it measured by the phenomenon?
claim: The question of originality concerns whether explication is imposed on or derived from the phenomenon

quote: These three aspects point to conceptuality without exhausting it
claim: The three methodological aspects (basic experience, guiding claim, intelligibility) indicate but do not exhaust conceptuality

quote: the basic experience in which I make the concrete character accessible to myself. This basic experience is primarily not theoretical
claim: The basic experience that makes concrete character accessible is primarily not theoretical

quote: but instead lies in the commerce of life with its world
claim: Basic experience lies in the commerce of life with its world, not in theoretical activity

quote: We will interrogate Aristotle's basic concepts from these three points of view
claim: Aristotle's basic concepts will be interrogated from the three methodological viewpoints

quote: We will see whether the matters meant by these basic concepts are thereby genuinely understood
claim: The purpose of the investigation is to see whether the matters meant by Aristotle's concepts are genuinely understood

quote: in conceptuality what constitutes the fulfillment of the questioning and determining of all scientific research is set in motion
claim: Conceptuality sets in motion what fulfills the questioning and determining of all scientific research

quote: It is not a matter of cognizance but of understanding
claim: The proper aim is understanding, not mere cognizance

quote: You have a genuine task to carry out: not of philosophizing but rather of becoming attentive, from where you are situated, to the conceptuality of a science
claim: The genuine task is not philosophizing but becoming attentive to the conceptuality of one's science from one's own situation

quote: to pursue it in such a way that the research fulfillment of conceptuality becomes vital
claim: The research fulfillment of conceptuality should become vital through proper pursuit

quote: It is not a matter of studying all of the scientific theories that periodically appear!
claim: Studying all periodically appearing scientific theories is not the proper task

quote: By paying attention to the proper fulfillment of a specific science, you attain a legitimate, proper, and serious relation to the matter of your science
claim: Attending to proper fulfillment of a specific science yields a legitimate and serious relation to that science's subject matter

quote: Not in such a way that you can apply Aristotelian concepts, but rather in doing for your science what Aristotle did in his place
claim: The goal is not to apply Aristotelian concepts but to do for one's own science what Aristotle did for his

quote: to see and to determine the matters with the same originality and le­gitimacy
claim: Aristotle saw and determined matters with originality and legitimacy, which should be emulated

quote: I simply have the task of providing the opportunity for Aristotle to put the matter before you
claim: Heidegger's task is to provide opportunity for Aristotle's matters to be presented

quote: it is necessary that we understand how this conceptuality holds the aforementioned aspects together, where they genuinely belong
claim: Understanding conceptuality requires grasping how it unifies basic experience, claim, and tendency toward intelligibility in their proper place

quote: We will have to seek out the indigenous character of conceptuality—for we want to understand not just any basic concepts, but Aristotle's
claim: Understanding Aristotle's basic concepts specifically requires investigating the indigenous character of conceptuality

quote: We will have to consult the way that Greek conceptuality and its indigenous character look
claim: Proper investigation requires examining the specific form of Greek conceptuality and its indigenous character

quote: Only then can we securely pursue the scientific explication as Aristotle conducted it
claim: Secure pursuit of Aristotelian scientific explication is conditional upon understanding Greek conceptuality's indigenous character

quote: By going back to what definition originally was, we might also learn what it originally was that one today designates as concept
claim: Returning to the original nature of definition can illuminate what is now called 'concept'

quote: Genus and species are characteristics that determine every definition
claim: Genus and species are determining characteristics of every definition

quote: However, they are not the only determining factors. These factors include the further moment of proprium and of differentia specifica
claim: Besides genus and species, proprium and differentia specifica are also determining factors in definition

quote: These aspects, which guide concept-formation, are called predicables or κατηγορήματα
claim: The aspects guiding concept-formation are termed predicables (κατηγορήματα)

quote: These κατηγορήματα were systematically treated for the first time by Porphyry in his introduction to Aristotle's Κατηγορίαι
claim: Porphyry was the first to systematically treat the predicables, in his introduction to Aristotle's Categories

quote: This Εἰσαγωγή was then translated into Latin by Boethius and became the basic text on logical questions in the Middle Ages
claim: Boethius translated Porphyry's Isagoge into Latin, and it became the foundational text for medieval logic

quote: The so-called controversy over universals of the Middle Ages developed in connection with this Εἰσαγωγή
claim: The medieval controversy over universals arose in connection with Porphyry's Isagoge

quote: There are five predicables
claim: The predicables number five in total

quote: Genus est unum, quod de pluribus specie differentibus in eo quod quid est praedicatur
claim: Genus is that which is predicated of many things differing in species with respect to what something is

quote: "Curved, closed line"—the genus of the circle—is predicated of many things that are distinct in species (ellipse)
claim: 'Curved, closed line' as genus of circle exemplifies predication of genus across species-distinct things like ellipses

quote: Still, the predicate captures what the circle in itself is
claim: The genus-predicate captures the essential nature of the circle

quote: Species est unum, quod de pluribus solo numero differentibus in eo quod quid est praedicatur
claim: Species is that which is predicated of many things differing only numerically with respect to what something is

quote: The individual circle solo numero differunt
claim: Individual circles differ from one another only numerically

quote: Differentia specifica aut διαφορά est unum, quod de pluribus praedicatur in quale essentiale
claim: Differentia specifica is that which is predicated of many things with respect to an essential quality

quote: "with respect to that which belongs to what they are," such as the rationality of the human being
claim: Differentia specifica refers to what essentially belongs to a thing, exemplified by rationality in humans

quote: Proprium est unum, quod de pluribus praedicatur in quale necessarium
claim: Proprium is that which is predicated of many things with respect to a necessary quality

quote: a "necessary" determination that belongs to the thing, but also lies outside of the essential context of genus and species
claim: Proprium is a necessary determination of a thing that falls outside the essential context of genus and species

quote: Accidens est unum, quod de pluribus praedicatur in quale contingens
claim: Accidens is that which is predicated of many things with respect to a contingent quality

quote: insofar as that which is addressed is "haphazard" (συμβεβηκός)
claim: Accidens addresses what is haphazard or contingent (συμβεβηκός)

quote: These praedicabilia are also called universalia
claim: The predicables are alternatively termed universals (universalia)

quote: universale means: unum quod est in pluribus
claim: The term 'universale' signifies 'one which is in many' (unum quod est in pluribus)

quote: praedicabile: unum quod de pluribus praedicatur
claim: The term 'praedicabile' signifies 'one which is predicated of many' (unum quod de pluribus praedicatur)

quote: the question of whether the general actually exists in the things or is only the generality of ap­prehending thought (Realism—Nominalism)
claim: The distinction between universale and praedicabile gives rise to the question of whether the general exists in things or only in apprehending thought

quote: This question also has its origin in determinate concrete contexts of Greek philosophy, or better in scholastic misunderstandings thereof
claim: The Realism-Nominalism question originates in Greek philosophical contexts or in scholastic misunderstandings of those contexts

quote: going back from definitio as technical instrument to ὁρισμός, "limitation."
claim: The investigation of conceptuality requires going back from 'definitio' as technical instrument to the Greek term 'ὁρισμός' meaning 'limitation'

quote: Ὁρισμός is a λόγος, a "speaking" about something, an addressing of the matter "itself in that which it is," καθ᾿ αὑτό
claim: ὁρισμός is a λόγος that addresses the matter itself in that which it is (καθ᾿ αὑτό)

quote: A λέγειν καθ᾿ αὑτό: the matter "in itself," and only it, is and should be addressed
claim: In λέγειν καθ᾿ αὑτό, the matter 'in itself' and only it should be addressed

quote: the ὁρισμός is determined as οὐσίας τις γνωρισμός
claim: ὁρισμός is determined as οὐσίας τις γνωρισμός (a certain making-known of being)

quote: Γνωρισμός means: "making known with . . . ," "making familiar with . . . ," presenting a matter
claim: Γνωρισμός means 'making known with,' 'making familiar with,' or presenting a matter

quote: Ὁρισμός is making one fa­miliar with a being in its being
claim: ὁρισμός is making one familiar with a being in its being

quote: Λόγος: "speaking," not in the sense of uttering a sound but speaking about something in a way that exhibits the about-which of speaking
claim: Λόγος means speaking not as uttering sounds but as speaking about something in a way that exhibits what is spoken about

quote: The genuine function of the λόγος is the ἀποφαίνεσθαι, the "bringing of a matter to sight."
claim: The genuine function of λόγος is ἀποφαίνεσθαι, the bringing of a matter to sight

quote: Every speaking is, above all for the Greeks, a speaking to someone or with others, with oneself or to oneself
claim: For the Greeks, every speaking is a speaking to someone, with others, with oneself, or to oneself

quote: Speaking is in concrete being-there, where one does not exist alone, speaking with others about something
claim: Speaking in concrete being-there (Dasein) is speaking with others about something, since one does not exist alone

quote: Speaking with others about something is, in each case, a speaking out of oneself
claim: Speaking with others about something is always a speaking out of oneself

quote: In speaking about something with others, I express myself (spreche ich mich aus), whether explicitly or not
claim: In speaking about something with others, one expresses oneself whether explicitly or not

quote: It is the fundamental determination of the being of the human being as such
claim: Λόγος is the fundamental determination of the being of the human being as such

quote: The human being is seen by the Greeks as ζῷον λόγον ἔχον, not only philosophically but in concrete living
claim: The Greeks understood the human being as ζῷον λόγον ἔχον both philosophically and in concrete living

quote: "a living thing that (as living) has language."
claim: ζῷον λόγον ἔχον means 'a living thing that (as living) has language'

quote: This definition should not be thought in biologi­cal, psychological, social-scientific, or any such terms
claim: The definition of human being as ζῷον λόγον ἔχον should not be thought in biological, psychological, or social-scientific terms

quote: This determination lies before such distinctions
claim: The determination of human being as ζῷον λόγον ἔχον is ontologically prior to biological, psychological, and social-scientific distinctions

quote: Ζωή is a concept of being; "life" refers to a mode of being, indeed a mode of being-in-a-world
claim: Ζωή is a concept of being; 'life' refers to a mode of being, specifically a mode of being-in-a-world

quote: A living thing is not simply at hand (vorhanden), but is in a world in that it has its world
claim: A living thing is not simply present-at-hand (vorhanden) but is in a world by having its world

quote: An animal is not simply moving down the road, pushed along by some mechanism. It is in the world in the sense of having it
claim: An animal is not merely mechanically propelled but is in the world in the sense of having it

quote: The being-in-the-world of the human being is determined in its ground through speaking
claim: The being-in-the-world of the human being is fundamentally determined through speaking

quote: The fundamental mode of being in which the human being is in its world is in speaking with it, about it, of it
claim: The fundamental mode of being in which the human being inhabits its world is speaking with, about, and of that world

quote: Thus is the human being determined precisely through the λόγος
claim: The human being is determined precisely through λόγος

quote: if definition is a λόγος, the matter of definition has its ground insofar as λόγος is the basic determination of the being of the human being
claim: If definition is a logos, then definition is grounded in logos being the basic determination of human being

quote: The λόγος as ὁρισμός addresses beings in their οὐσία, in their being-there
claim: Logos as horismos (definition) addresses beings in their ousia, their being-there

quote: Therefore, we must gain an understanding of οὐσία
claim: Understanding ousia is necessary for understanding logos as definition

quote: The conceptuality meant in the basic concepts is a concretely giving basic experience, not a theoretical grasping of the matter
claim: Conceptuality in basic concepts is a concrete giving basic experience rather than theoretical grasping

quote: That which is so experienced is addressed to something
claim: What is experienced in basic concepts is addressed to something

quote: What is thus experienced and posited in this regard becomes explicit and becomes vital in the address
claim: What is experienced and posited becomes explicit and vital through address

quote: We must recover the indigenous character as it became vital in Greek science
claim: Recovering the indigenous character of concepts as vital in Greek science is methodologically necessary

quote: In the definition, the concept becomes explicit; it comes to light
claim: Definition makes the concept explicit; it brings the concept to light

quote: Definition: proximate genus and specific difference
claim: Definition consists of proximate genus and specific difference

quote: We want to understand what definition means by questioning back to what it meant for the Greeks, for Aristotle
claim: Understanding definition requires questioning back to its meaning for the Greeks and Aristotle

quote: Ὁρισμός: 'circumscription,' 'delimitation.'
claim: Horismos means circumscription or delimitation

quote: Ὁρισμός: λόγος ουσίας
claim: Horismos is logos of ousia

quote: By clarifying that, we will find the indigenous character of the concept
claim: Clarifying logos, ousia, and logos ousias will reveal the indigenous character of the concept

quote: In traditional scholastic language, concepts are (1) notio, (2) intentio, (3) conceptus, (4) species
claim: Scholastic tradition designates concepts by four terms: notio, intentio, conceptus, species

quote: notio: In the concept lies a definite 'acquaintance' with the matter meant by it
claim: Notio signifies that the concept contains definite acquaintance with the matter meant

quote: the concept is transposed within a being-acquainted
claim: The concept is situated within a mode of being-acquainted

quote: intentio: In the concept lies an 'aiming' at, an intending of something
claim: Intentio signifies that the concept contains an aiming-at or intending of something

quote: Intending a matter is an essential structural aspect of the concept
claim: Intending a matter is an essential structural aspect of the concept

quote: conceptus: The 'grasping.' The matter is not only intended, not only something with which one is acquainted
claim: Conceptus signifies grasping: the matter is not merely intended or acquainted with

quote: one intends it and is acquainted with it in the mode of its being-grasped, so that what lies in it is embraced, gathered
claim: In conceptus, one intends and is acquainted with something in the mode of being-grasped, embracing and gathering what lies in it

quote: species: εἶδος, 'look'; this leads back to notio
claim: Species means eidos or look, and it leads back to notio

quote: If I am acquainted with the matter, I know how it looks, how it appears as such among others
claim: Being acquainted with a matter means knowing how it looks and appears among others

quote: These designations have acquired a customary meaning in their scholastic application, so that they are uniformly translated as 'concept.'
claim: The four scholastic designations have acquired customary meanings and are uniformly translated as 'concept'

quote: Definition should be viewed with regard to its origin: λόγος ουσίας
claim: Definition should be understood through its origin as logos ousias

quote: Λόγος, for the Greeks, is the 'speaking' and at the same time the 'spoken'
claim: For the Greeks, logos means both the act of speaking and what is spoken

quote: speaking in the basic function of ἀποφαίνεσθαι or δηλοῦν
claim: Speaking has the basic function of apophainesthai or deloun

quote: 'a bringing-a-matter-to-self-showing' in speaking about something
claim: Apophainesthai/deloun means bringing a matter to self-showing through speaking about something

quote: This speaking about something is its tendency toward speaking with others, self-expressing
claim: Speaking about something has a tendency toward speaking with others and self-expressing

quote: In speaking with others and with myself, I bring what is addressed to givenness for me
claim: Speaking with others and oneself brings what is addressed to givenness
